items.readable_text:
Content:
In this lesson, we learn how to conduct hypothesis tests to evaluate whether sufficient evidence exists that two variances from normal populations are equal.

Content:
Suppose we have two independent normal populations [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X\sim N(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x), \qquad Y\sim N(\mu_y, \sigma^2_y)]

Content:
We conduct a sample of size [MATH: n_x] from [MATH: X] and a sample of size [MATH: n_y] from [MATH: Y.]

Content:
Let [MATH: W_\nu] denote a chi-square random variable with [MATH: \nu] degrees of freedom, i.e.
[MATH: W_\nu \sim \chi^2(\nu).]

Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw that
[MATH: W_{n_x-1} = \dfrac{(n_x-1)S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x}, \qquad W_{n_y-1} = \dfrac{(n_y-1)S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y}]
where [MATH: S_x^2] and [MATH: S_y^2] are the sample variances.

Content:
Additionally, by the definition of the [MATH: F]-distribution, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{W_{\nu_1} / \nu_1}{W_{\nu_2} / \nu_2} \sim F(\nu_1, \nu_2).]

Content:
To define a critical region, we first need a test statistic whose distribution is known under the null hypothesis. In this case, a natural choice for the statistic is the ratio of the sample variances:
[MATH: \frac{S_x^2 }{ S_y^2}]

Content:
But what is the distribution of this ratio?

Content:
As we will see, it is easier to analyze the distribution of the standardized ratio
[MATH: \frac{{S_x^2}/{\sigma_x^2}}{{S_y^2}/{\sigma_y^2}}.]

Content:
Under the null hypothesis [MATH: \sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2], so under [MATH: H_0] our ratio coincides with the standardized one. This is why studying the standardized form allows us to determine the critical region for the test.

Content:
Our goal is to find the probability distribution of
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{S_y^2/\sigma^2_y}.]

Content:
Using the relationship between the sample variance and chi-square distributions, we can write
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x} = \dfrac{ (n_x-1)S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{n_x-1}]
and similarly
[MATH: \dfrac{S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ (n_y-1)S_y^2/\sigma^2_y}{n_y-1}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x} = \dfrac{ W_{n_x-1} }{n_x-1}, \qquad \dfrac{S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ W_{n_y-1}}{n_y-1}.]

Content:
So, if we divide [MATH: S_x^2/\sigma^2_x] by [MATH: S_y^2/\sigma^2_y,] this is simply the ratio of two chi-square random variables scaled by their respective degrees of freedom.

Content:
Therefore, by the definition of the [MATH: F]-distribution, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{S_y^2/\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ W_{n_x-1}/(n_x-1) }{ W_{n_y-1}/(n_y-1) } \sim F(n_x-1, n_y-1).]

Content:
Let's summarize this result:

Content:
> Given two random samples from independent normal populations [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] the random variable
> [MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma_x^2}{S_y^2/\sigma_y^2}]
> follows the [MATH: F]-distribution with [MATH: \nu_x = n_x-1] and [MATH: \nu_y = n_y-1] degrees of freedom, where
>
> - [MATH: S_x^2] and [MATH: S_y^2] are the sample variances,
> - [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2] are the population variances,
> - [MATH: n_x] and [MATH: n_y] are the sample sizes.
>
> Furthermore, if [MATH: \sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2,] we have
> [MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{S_y^2} \sim F(\nu_x, \nu_y).]

items.title: Reformulating as a Right-Tailed Test

sections.normalized_html: When conducting hypothesis tests for variances, we usually work with the right-tailed critical values of the [MATH: F]-Distribution. For this reason, we should always divide the larger variance by the smaller one when calculating our test statistic.
sections.readable_text: When conducting hypothesis tests for variances, we usually work with the right-tailed critical values of the [MATH: F]-Distribution. For this reason, we should always divide the larger variance by the smaller one when calculating our test statistic.

• If our alternative hypothesis is [MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_x^2 > \sigma_y^2] then, we find our right-tailed test statistic [MATH: f] by calculating the ratio [MATH: f = \dfrac{s_x^2}{s_y^2}] where [MATH: s_x^2] and [MATH: s_y^2] are the usual unbiased estimates of [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2,] respectively.

  • On the other hand, if our alternative hypothesis is [MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_x^2 < \sigma_y^2] then, we can rewrite this as [MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_y^2 > \sigma_x^2] in which case, the right-tailed test statistic is given by [MATH: f = \dfrac{s_y^2}{s_x^2}.]

  • Similarly, if the alternative hypothesis is [MATH: \sigma^2_x \neq \sigma^2_y,] we can conduct a right-tailed test by dividing the larger sample variance by the smaller.

We are told that the two populations are independent and normally distributed, but we do not know the population variances [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2.]

Given two random samples from independent normal populations [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] the random variable

[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma_x^2}{S_y^2/\sigma_y^2}] follows an [MATH: F]-distribution with [MATH: \nu_x = n_x-1] and [MATH: \nu_y = n_y-1] degrees of freedom, where

  • [MATH: S_x^2] and [MATH: S_y^2] are the sample variances,

  • [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2] are the population variances,

  • [MATH: n_x] and [MATH: n_y] are the sample sizes.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we learn how to conduct hypothesis tests to evaluate whether sufficient evidence exists that two variances from normal populations are equal.

Content:
Suppose we have two independent normal populations [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X\sim N(\mu_x, \sigma^2_x), \qquad Y\sim N(\mu_y, \sigma^2_y)]

Content:
We conduct a sample of size [MATH: n_x] from [MATH: X] and a sample of size [MATH: n_y] from [MATH: Y.]

Content:
Let [MATH: W_\nu] denote a chi-square random variable with [MATH: \nu] degrees of freedom, i.e.
[MATH: W_\nu \sim \chi^2(\nu).]

Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw that
[MATH: W_{n_x-1} = \dfrac{(n_x-1)S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x}, \qquad W_{n_y-1} = \dfrac{(n_y-1)S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y}]
where [MATH: S_x^2] and [MATH: S_y^2] are the sample variances.

Content:
Additionally, by the definition of the [MATH: F]-distribution, we have

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{W_{\nu_1} / \nu_1}{W_{\nu_2} / \nu_2} \sim F(\nu_1, \nu_2).]

Content:
To define a critical region, we first need a test statistic whose distribution is known under the null hypothesis. In this case, a natural choice for the statistic is the ratio of the sample variances:
[MATH: \frac{S_x^2 }{ S_y^2}]

Content:
But what is the distribution of this ratio?

Content:
As we will see, it is easier to analyze the distribution of the standardized ratio
[MATH: \frac{{S_x^2}/{\sigma_x^2}}{{S_y^2}/{\sigma_y^2}}.]

Content:
Under the null hypothesis [MATH: \sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2], so under [MATH: H_0] our ratio coincides with the standardized one. This is why studying the standardized form allows us to determine the critical region for the test.

Content:
Our goal is to find the probability distribution of
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{S_y^2/\sigma^2_y}.]

Content:
Using the relationship between the sample variance and chi-square distributions, we can write
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x} = \dfrac{ (n_x-1)S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{n_x-1}]
and similarly
[MATH: \dfrac{S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ (n_y-1)S_y^2/\sigma^2_y}{n_y-1}.]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{\sigma^2_x} = \dfrac{ W_{n_x-1} }{n_x-1}, \qquad \dfrac{S_y^2}{\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ W_{n_y-1}}{n_y-1}.]

Content:
So, if we divide [MATH: S_x^2/\sigma^2_x] by [MATH: S_y^2/\sigma^2_y,] this is simply the ratio of two chi-square random variables scaled by their respective degrees of freedom.

Content:
Therefore, by the definition of the [MATH: F]-distribution, we have
[MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma^2_x}{S_y^2/\sigma^2_y} = \dfrac{ W_{n_x-1}/(n_x-1) }{ W_{n_y-1}/(n_y-1) } \sim F(n_x-1, n_y-1).]

Content:
Let's summarize this result:

Content:
> Given two random samples from independent normal populations [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] the random variable
> [MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2/\sigma_x^2}{S_y^2/\sigma_y^2}]
> follows the [MATH: F]-distribution with [MATH: \nu_x = n_x-1] and [MATH: \nu_y = n_y-1] degrees of freedom, where
>
> - [MATH: S_x^2] and [MATH: S_y^2] are the sample variances,
> - [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2] are the population variances,
> - [MATH: n_x] and [MATH: n_y] are the sample sizes.
>
> Furthermore, if [MATH: \sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2,] we have
> [MATH: \dfrac{S_x^2}{S_y^2} \sim F(\nu_x, \nu_y).]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Reformulating as a Right-Tailed Test

Content:
When conducting hypothesis tests for variances, we usually work with the right-tailed critical values of the [MATH: F]-Distribution. For this reason, we should always divide the larger variance by the smaller one when calculating our test statistic.

Content:
For example,

Content:
- If our alternative hypothesis is
[MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_x^2 > \sigma_y^2]
then, we find our right-tailed test statistic [MATH: f] by calculating the ratio
[MATH: f = \dfrac{s_x^2}{s_y^2}]
where [MATH: s_x^2] and [MATH: s_y^2] are the usual unbiased estimates of [MATH: \sigma_x^2] and [MATH: \sigma_y^2,] respectively.
- On the other hand, if our alternative hypothesis is
[MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_x^2 < \sigma_y^2]
then, we can rewrite this as
[MATH: H_1:\:\sigma_y^2 > \sigma_x^2]
in which case, the right-tailed test statistic is given by
[MATH: f = \dfrac{s_y^2}{s_x^2}.]
- Similarly, if the alternative hypothesis is [MATH: \sigma^2_x \neq \sigma^2_y,] we can conduct a right-tailed test by dividing the larger sample variance by the smaller.

Content:
Let's see some examples.

---
